title: Longest Subsequence With a Fixed Difference

concept.title: A table indexed by the last value
body: A **subsequence** keeps the order of the elements but may skip some. You look for the longest subsequence in which every element is exactly `d` more than the previous one (`d` can be negative or 0). Let `dp[x]` be the length of the longest such subsequence that **ends with the value `x`**. When you read a new element `x`, the best subsequence ending at `x` extends the best one that ends at `x - d`:

The values can be huge, so `dp` is a **hash map** (an array indexed by value would be far too big). Because the elements are read from left to right, `dp[x - d]` only contains subsequences that used earlier elements. For `d = 0` the answer is the largest number of equal elements; the formula still works because `dp[x - 0]` is read before `dp[x]` is updated.

statement: Given `n` integers and a number `d`, find the length of the longest subsequence (elements in their original order, not necessarily next to each other) in which each element is exactly `d` larger than the one before it.

examples.note: The subsequences 5 7 and 1 3 have length 2; there is no subsequence of length 3.

hints: Let dp[x] be the longest valid subsequence ending with value x.
A new element x extends the best subsequence that ends with x - d.
Use a hash map for dp, since the values are large.

explanation: `dp[x]` is the longest valid subsequence ending with `x`; a new element extends the one ending with `x - d`. The map holds `dp`, and the best value seen is the answer.
solution.complexity: Time O(n) on average, space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, d = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

dp = {}
best = 0
for x in a:
    dp[x] = dp.get(x - d, 0) + 1
    best = max(best, dp[x])
print(best)
